title: Show HN: Cubic Doggo 07B Wouf: A low-cost open-source quadruped with ST3215
author: SphericalCowww
body:
Cubic Doggo 07B Wouf is a ROS2-controlled 12-DOF untethered quadruped, built with ST3215 smart servos fully with off-the-shelf components and 3D-printed partsFeaturing:
* 12 ST-3215-C018 servos, usually on a bundled sale because of SO-ARM101
* Walking forward with a payload of 1 kg
* Smart servos as required for closed-loop reinforcement learning capability 
* FreeCAD models fully available for editing
* M3 screws and locknuts are used extensively (instead of glue or heat set inserts) to strengthen and secure the PLA+ printed structures. Design iterates on strengthening whichever part breaks first. Check JLCPCB for stronger components
* No custom PCB (because I am terrible at it), only 2 required soldering points
* Runs on a Raspberry Pi with ROS2 Jazzy installed. Joystick control ready
* Walks on batteries
* Aesthetics of an exposed electronic box, but great as a development platform for stacking new components on top

Domestic gardens make up an almost insignificant percentage of their natural habitat in any case, and any sort of HOA or Estate Management scenario would likely make it a violation to rewild a garden sufficient to create an amenable hedgehog habitat.

In short, its the responsibility of land utilised for agriculture - and this is recognised by measures around Europe such as the Eco-Scheme and ACRES (Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme) which indirectly support the re-establishment of hedgehog populations.

- be waterproof against rain

I know very little about the drama around Britney Spears, but even I know that the question was if her conservator was abusing it, not "the deep state". It's a case of the breach of trust of one or a very few people, NOT a grand conspiracy requiring a supernatural level of coordination and control. title: Show HN: I created a spreadsheet in a plain text file
author: zbian
body: I built a plain-text spreadsheet format and an app for working with it.It began with small tasks like tracking my dog's health records and organizing records for tax season. Full spreadsheet apps always felt excessive, while Markdown tables don't support formulas.Also, its compact and readable syntax lets AI read and edit a workbook directly, without spreadsheet-specific tools. You can try the in-app agent on the desktop version with ChatGPT sign-in.Ordinate is now open source and available to try. My hope is for it to do for spreadsheets what Markdown did for documents.For more about it: https://ordinate.dev

comments.author: andunie
comments.text: This is amazing.I used to have many ideas in my mind for an open embeddable spreadsheets implementation, this is one of the cases I didn't have in mind, but it's pretty great and would fix LLMs outputting xls files for the most mundane tasks.

title: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer
author: falperc
body: Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!It can talk(kinda)You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

title: Show HN: InputConfig, a free open-source app to run your Mac with any controller
author: ryleighnewman
body:
# ryleighnewman/InputConfig

Free, open-source controller mapper for macOS. Map any game controller to keyboard and mouse: PS5 DualSense, Xbox, Switch Pro, 8BitDo, even MIDI, and any HID gamepad. No drivers, built for accessibility.

- Stars: 149
- Forks: 8
- Watchers: 149
- Open issues: 2
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: https://inputconfig.com
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-04-09T03:49:38Z

## Languages

- Python
- Shell
- Swift

## Topics

- 8bitdo
- accessibility
- adaptive-controller
- controller-mapper
- controller-mapping
- dualsense
- dualshock
- game-controller
- gamepad
- gamepad-mapper
- input-remapping
- joystick
- keyboard-mapping
- macos
- macos-app
- midi
- nintendo-switch-pro-controller
- swift
- swiftui
- xbox-controller

## Top Contributors

- ryleighnewman (51 contributions)

---

## README

# InputConfig: free controller mapper for Mac

Turn literally anything into your Mac's input

InputConfig is a free, open-source controller mapper for macOS. Map any PS5, Xbox or
Switch controller to keyboard keys and mouse movement, use a controller as a mouse,
run your Mac from a MIDI knob box, play games that never supported controllers, or
replace a keyboard entirely if using one is difficult. It works in every app, not
only games.

Works with PS5 DualSense and DualSense Edge, PS4 DualShock 4, Xbox Wireless, Series
and Elite, Switch Pro, Switch 2 and Joy-Con, 8BitDo Pro 2 and Ultimate 2C, the PlayStation Access Controller, the
Xbox Adaptive Controller, MIDI keyboards and pad controllers, and any HID-compatible
gamepad. No drivers, no subscription, no account.

Website and documentation: inputconfig.com, with
help for every feature, guides,
and ready-made presets for 450+ games and apps.

 

## Overview

Plug in your device, pick a preset, and go. Or build your own from scratch: every
button, trigger, stick, key, knob, and pad can send keys, clicks, mouse motion,
scroll, macros, MIDI, spoken phrases, or a system function like volume, brightness,
or a Siri Shortcut.

It is not just for game controllers. Your Mac keyboard, a second keyboard, extra
mouse buttons, the trackpad (including Force Touch pressure), regions of the screen,
and full MIDI gear all work as inputs too.

## What's new in 1.8

- Access controller: Socket 1 to 8, the stick, the center, PS and Profile buttons, and whatever is plugged into E1 to E4 are read by name, over USB-C and Bluetooth
- Access profiles: a Profile chip in the Live Visualizer lists the three stored profiles over USB-C, switches them, and edits one beside the drawing with the PS5's own settings
- Controller Profile, a new output: a row switches an Access controller to the next, previous, or a numbered profile
- DualSense Edge: its four stored profiles are read over USB-C and listed with what each one remaps
- Trigger feel: click L2 or R2 in the Live Visualizer of a DualSense or DualSense Edge for light, medium or firm resistance
- Switch 2 controllers over Bluetooth: with the new Devices setting on, a paired Switch 2 Pro, GameCube or Joy-Con 2 controller is read wirelessly; Joy-Con 2 are read over USB in the grip too
- Switch 2 Pro and GameCube controllers read their stick and trigger calibration and their motion sensors from the controller
- Xbox pads over Bluetooth: Share works on every firmware, Elite Series 2 paddles and profiles are read, and the Devices menu names the pads macOS does not read over USB
- Pen tablets: pressure, tilt, pen buttons, eraser and in range are inputs of their own
- Contour ShuttlePRO and 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse are read, jog, shuttle and all six axes included
- Triple tap: a row can do something else on three quick taps, beside its hold and double tap actions
- Wireless controllers: optionally disconnect a controller after it sits unused for 5 to 60 minutes, and try to reconnect paired controllers when the app opens, the Mac wakes or a preset starts

Full release history in CHANGELOG.md. This section tracks the latest release.

## A tour

Open InputConfig and everything it can do is on one screen. Controllers, keyboards,
mice, trackpads, and MIDI gear go in; keys, mouse, macros, MIDI, system functions,
and Siri Shortcuts come out. Forty-six presets ship with it, sorted into folders you
can name and color, and the Smart Preset Maker draws on a library of more than 450
games and apps.

Press anything to bind it

Scanning maps any input the instant you touch it. No manual codes, no guesswork,
and it works for controllers, MIDI gear, and your Mac's own keyboard and trackpad.

Fine-tune every binding

One press can send a key, a click, a MIDI note, and a spoken phrase at once, then
repeat while held, send Return on a double tap, run a two-step macro, and rumble,
with every timing set right in the row.

Your Mac is an input, too

Every key on the keyboard, every click, scroll gesture, and Force Touch on the
trackpad or mouse, any area of the screen, and a knock on the palm rest can all be
scanned and mapped like a controller button.

Built for accessibility

Drive your whole Mac from a single stick. One-stick driving steers, accelerates,
brakes, and shifts from one control, and it outputs keyboard and mouse, so it works
in games that never planned for it. Built with the PlayStation Access Controller
and other adaptive hardware in mind.

Send MIDI in and out

Play notes into your DAW through a virtual MIDI port, or let a MIDI keyboard or knob
box drive the Mac itself: volume, tracks, brightness, Mission Control, a Siri
Shortcut. Every binding shows exactly what it sends.

See every input live

The Live Visualizer mirrors your controller and your MIDI gear in real time. Sticks,
triggers, keys, and knobs light up as you play, clicking any control jumps straight
to its binding, and Edit Layout rearranges the keyboard, mouse, touchpad and generic
maps; a drawn controller keeps its real layout.

Draw regions on any control

Draw regions right in the editor: rings on a stick, bands along a trigger's pull, and
areas on a controller touchpad or the screen. Each region is a button of its own, and
the Live Visualizer lights it as you reach it.

Dial in gyro and deadzones

Set the Deadzone and Full push at points on every stick and trigger and watch the row
follow live, so drift disappears and full travel stays. Bind gyroscope rotation to the mouse for
motion aim in any app, with live sensor readings and a resting-zero calibration.

Open source, yours

No accounts, no tracking, no locked features. Built by one person who needed it.

## How it compares

| | InputConfig | Joystick Mapper | Gamepad Companion | Enjoyable | Karabiner-Elements |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cost | Free | Paid | Paid | Free | Free |
| Open source | Yes, MIT | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| Game controllers | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No, keyboards only |
| MIDI keyboards and pads as input | Yes | No | No | No | No |
| Mac keyboard/mouse/trackpad as input | Yes | No | No | No | Keyboard only |
| DualSense Edge paddles and extras | Yes | No | No | No | No |
| System functions and Siri Shortcuts | Yes | No | No | No | Limited |
| Per-app preset switching | Yes | No | No | No | Yes |
| Macros, turbo, tap and hold | Yes | Limited | Limited | No | Limited |
| MIDI output | Yes | No | No | No | No |
| Gyroscope and motion | Yes | No | No | No | No |
| Light bar control | Yes | No | No | No | No |
| Still updated | Yes | Rarely | Rarely | No | Yes |

Checked August 2026. Some of these have been around far longer than mine and are good
tools. Check for yourself before you switch.

## Everything it does

### Input sources

- Every button, trigger, joystick, and D-pad on any MFi or HID-compatible gamepad
- DualSense Edge extras: both back paddles, both FN buttons, and the mute button, over USB and Bluetooth
- Controller touchpads: cursor control, two-finger tracking, regions, and one-finger and two-finger taps
- Gyroscope, accelerometer, and absolute attitude on Sony controllers (DualSense, DualShock 4)
- MIDI notes and pads, CC knobs, sliders, and pedals, the pitch wheel, channel and polyphonic aftertouch, Program Change, and transport Start, Continue, and Stop, from any MIDI device over USB or Bluetooth
- Three knob modes for MIDI dials: Switch (fires past halfway), Dial (speed grows from center, like a stick), and Turn (a nudge per step of rotation, for knobs and for endless encoders set to absolute mode)
- Per-binding MIDI channel and device filters, so two keyboards stay independent
- Your Mac keyboard as an input: every key, including Shift, Control, Option, Command, Caps Lock, fn, and the brightness, media, and volume keys, on the built-in keyboard or any keyboard you connect (all keyboards read as one)
- Your mouse and trackpad as inputs: every button, double click, scroll in four directions, scroll gestures, Force Touch pressure, and Force Click
- Tap the Mac: knock on the palm rest and the MacBook's motion sensor fires any output, single to quintuple taps, with a live calibration plot
- Screen regions: areas of any display that act as inputs while the pointer is inside them, per display or on every display
- Bluetooth headset and hearing aid buttons as media keys
- Switches, pedals, and sticks plugged into a PlayStation Access Controller or Xbox Adaptive Controller
- Stick regions as rings, trigger bands, and stick gestures such as pulling a stick back twice, each with its own bindings

### Outputs

- Keyboard keys, including full modifier combos (Cmd+Shift+3 and friends fire as real chords)
- Type whole words or phrases from a single press
- Mouse buttons, analog mouse motion, smooth scrolling, and single scroll steps
- Macro sequences with custom timing, chord steps that hold one key while tapping others, and interrupt-on-release
- MIDI out to your DAW through a virtual port: notes with velocity, CC, pitch bend, Program Change, and transport (start, stop, continue)
- Spoken phrases, in the system voice or any installed voice
- Haptic feedback with adjustable strength and duration
- App actions: switch presets, jump to a specific preset, pause and resume output, all from the controller

### System functions

- Volume up, volume down, and mute, in the same steps as the keyboard keys
- System volume as a fader: the Mac's level follows a knob's position 1-to-1, and only takes over once you actually move it
- Play/pause, next track, and previous track, as real media keys
- Screen brightness up and down
- Mission Control, Launchpad, Spotlight, lock screen, and the screenshot toolbar
- Run any Siri Shortcut by name, picked from a list of your installed Shortcuts, without stealing focus
- Open any app or any URL, from https links to app schemes

### Per-binding control

- Toggle mode: press once to latch, press again to release
- Turbo with an adjustable rate, and repeat counts with custom delays
- Hold actions and double-tap actions, each with their own outputs and timing windows
- Chords: a row can require up to three controls held together, each chosen from the menu or scanned
- Deadzone and Full push at on every stick and trigger, shown live in the row and in a full calibrator
- Axis inversion and three sensitivity curves: linear, smooth, aggressive
- Variable sensitivity: trigger pressure and stick depth scale the output speed
- Stacked outputs: one input firing several outputs in parallel
- A note field on every binding, so a preset explains itself

### Presets

- 46 built-in presets: Easy Browse and Easy Edit, an Auto Clicker, the Access Controller and One-Stick Driving, the Mac's own keyboard, trackpad, and modifiers, desktop navigation, web browsing, media control, popular games, MIDI and creative work, and feature showcases, every row annotated
- Smart Preset Maker builds a tailored preset from a few questions, from a library of more than 450 games, apps, and workflows, and can add a touchpad-as-trackpad, gyro fine aim, and trigger rumble
- Folders with names and colors, and unlimited presets of your own
- Per-app auto-switch: presets activate themselves when their app comes to the front
- Per-preset automation: launch an app or URL on activate, confine the cursor, auto-recenter, hide the pointer
- Import, export, and share presets, and convert them between controller types
- A global keyboard shortcut to toggle the most recent preset from anywhere
- Crash recovery offers to start your active preset again after a crash

### Live Visualizer

- A real-time mirror of every connected device, one panel per slot
- Switchable layouts per slot: controller, keyboard, mouse and trackpad, controller touchpad, screen regions, or MIDI instrument, with auto-detection from the bindings
- The MIDI instrument: a seven-octave velocity-shaded keyboard, a named dial for every knob (Mod Wheel, Cutoff, Sustain and the rest), knob-mode badges, pitch bend and aftertouch meters, a 16-channel activity strip, and a rolling event log
- Click any control to jump straight to its binding in the editor
- Edit Layout to rearrange the keyboard, mouse, touchpad and generic maps (a drawn controller keeps its real layout), plus zoom, pan, and four backgrounds
- A keyboard map in the shape of your keyboard, ANSI, ISO or JIS, with every key labeled in your own layout

### Accessibility

- One-stick driving: steer, accelerate, brake, and shift from a single stick
- App-wide text size, bold text, reduced transparency, and reduced motion, layered on top of the system settings
- VoiceOver support throughout, including the Live Visualizer spoken in plain words
- Built-in presets for the PlayStation Access Controller: Access Controller runs the whole desktop from one stick and eight sockets, and One-Stick Driving drives a whole car from one stick
- Deadzone and sensitivity tuning that matters for tremor and limited range of motion

### The app

- Light bar colors per preset with a full RGB picker, brightness control, and an RGB cycle, over USB and Bluetooth
- Battery level and connection state for every controller
- A changelog inside the app and a What's New popup after updates
- 42 built-in help guides, the same pages as inputconfig.com, and a guided Quick Start tour
- Available in 26 languages, with Arabic and Hebrew reading right to left
- Search in long dropdowns and in the sidebar, which also sorts by name or by date
- Menu bar control with a choice of twelve icons, plus Dock-only and menu-bar-only modes
- An activity log of everything the app does, with a one-file report ready to send
- Adjustable polling rate: 60, 120, 180, or 240 Hz, with an automatic battery saver
- Sandboxed, no network access, no telemetry

100% free.

## Supported controllers

- PlayStation Access Controller, with its sockets, expansion ports and stored profiles (and other adaptive hardware)
- PlayStation DualSense (PS5) and DualSense Edge, including the Edge's paddles, extra buttons and stored profiles
- PlayStation DualShock 4 (PS4)
- Xbox Wireless Controller (One, Series X|S), Xbox Elite Series 2, and the Xbox Adaptive Controller
- Nintendo Switch Pro Controller and Joy-Cons, and the Switch 2 Pro, Joy-Con 2 and GameCube controllers
- 8BitDo Pro 2, SN30 Pro+, SN30 Pro, and Ultimate 2C
- Steam Controller (2015 and 2026), Stadia Controller, the Logitech G29, G920 and G923 wheels, and Thrustmaster wheels
- Any MFi or HID-compatible gamepad, GP2040-CE boards and fight sticks included
- Pen tablets, the Contour ShuttlePRO and the 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse
- MIDI keyboards, pad controllers, knob boxes, and control surfaces
- Stream Deck keys, and the Stream Deck + dials and touch strip
- Your Mac keyboard, mouse, and trackpad

Other controllers, joysticks and wheels are read as well, shown in a generic drawing.

## Questions people ask

**How do I use a PS5 or Xbox controller as a keyboard and mouse on Mac?**
Install InputConfig, plug in or pair the controller, pick a preset, and press Activate.
macOS will ask for Accessibility permission the first time, which is what lets any app send
keystrokes and mouse movement.

**Can I use a MIDI keyboard or pad controller to control my Mac?**
Yes, and it needs no game controller alongside it. Notes and pads act like buttons,
knobs get three modes (Switch, Dial, Turn), the sustain pedal is a switch, and a knob
bound to System Volume becomes a hardware volume fader. The built-in MIDI: Knob Deck
and MIDI: Media Deck presets are ready to remap.

**Can I map the DualSense Edge back paddles and FN buttons?**
Yes. The Edge's back paddles, both FN buttons, and the mute button are bindable like
any other input, over both USB and Bluetooth. Over USB-C the app also reads its four stored
profiles and lists what each one remaps.

**Can a button run a Siri Shortcut or change the volume?**
Yes. System Functions are outputs like any other: volume, mute, media keys,
brightness, Mission Control, lock screen, the screenshot toolbar, any Siri Shortcut
by name, or opening any app or URL.

**Is there a free alternative to Joystick Mapper or Gamepad Companion?**
This is one. InputConfig is free with nothing locked, and the source is public under MIT.

**Can I use a controller instead of a keyboard and mouse entirely?**
Yes, that is the point. There are built-in presets for desktop navigation, web browsing,
and media control, plus presets built for adaptive controllers. You can map screen regions,
type whole phrases from one button, and switch presets automatically per app.

**Does it work with the PlayStation Access Controller or the Xbox Adaptive Controller?**
Yes, along with anything else that presents as an MFi or HID gamepad, and the switches,
pedals, and sticks plugged into their ports are inputs too. The Access Controller preset
runs the whole desktop from one stick and eight sockets, and One-Stick Driving lets a
single stick handle steering, throttle, braking, and gear changes. Accessibility is why the app exists, not an
afterthought.

**Do I need drivers?**
No. Connect the controller by USB or Bluetooth and macOS handles the rest. MIDI
devices are found automatically too. Wired Xbox One and Series pads need macOS 15
or later; on macOS 14, connect them over Bluetooth.

**Can I map a controller for a game that has no controller support?**
Yes. Map the buttons and sticks to whatever keys and mouse motion the game expects, and it
sees a normal keyboard and mouse.

**Is it really free?**
Yes. No paid tier, no trial, no locked features. There is a tip jar in the app that unlocks
nothing.

## Requirements

- macOS 14.0 or later
- Accessibility permission (for keyboard and mouse simulation)
- Tap the Mac needs an Apple silicon MacBook: desktop Macs and Intel Macs have no motion sensor, and some earlier models do not publish it. On macOS 27 the Mac App Store sandbox does not let InputConfig switch the motion sensor on, so taps are heard while the sensor is already on

## Building

1. Open `InputConfig.xcodeproj` in Xcode 26 or later
2. Select your team in Signing & Capabilities
3. Build and run

## License

MIT License. See LICENSE for details.

## Acknowledgments

- SDL_GameControllerDB and SDL, Copyright (C) 1997-2025 Sam Lantinga, used under the zlib license. The full notice is in `SDLGameControllerDBData.swift`.
- procon2-mac, Copyright (c) 2026 Arda Caglayan Ercan, used under the MIT License, for the Switch 2 controller USB start-up commands. The full license text is in `Switch2USBEnabler.swift`.

## Privacy

InputConfig does not collect any data. See PRIVACY.md.

## Contact

Questions, bugs, or feature requests? Open an issue here, see inputconfig.com/help, or reach out at ryleighnewman.com.

title: Show HN: KernelCash – Privacy First Budgeting
author: LoftyHobbitMan
body:
Hi everyone! I typically do not put my projects out for others to see, so this is new to me, but I have created a privacy first budgeting app called KernelCash Budgets ( https://kernelcash.com ), and wanted to share it here in the event someone was interested in a product like this. This app has really helped my wife and I, as well as some family, friends, and colleagues, so I wanted to put this out to see if it could help anyone else.I created this app as a replacement to some of the other budgeting apps out there. Some of KernelCash's core features include:- Envelope and zero style budgeting
- Expense, income, and savings goal tracking
- Full analytics for income, expenses, and savings
- Bank connection / sync free. We use transaction file imports (OFX / QFX) or manual entry to keep things private. You can freely share or not share what you choose.
- Multi-collaborator workspaces. These are great for sharing your budget with a spouse, roommates, and have even been used by some parents to teach their kids how to budget. Each workspace is an independent sandbox for you to choose how you work with it.
- Customizable budgets that are not month-locked. You control the time span of each budget you have.
- There is only one pricing tier so you will always get every feature.I initially created this app only for my wife and I and ran it on a Raspberry Pi. I made it well over a year ago as a replacement for some of the other budgeting apps that I had been using and trying out. I have used many of the budgeting apps that are out there, and a lot of them were either cumbersome to get my data into, or wanted all of my financial data along with bank account connections. Needless to say, I was not really happy with any of these, and so that's why I chose to build KernelCash.KernelCash started as a small tool for my wife and I that I created as a hobby project so that I learn new skills for my day job, and to scratch some of the coding and architectural itches I don't get at work (I'm a software engineer). I never intended to release this to the public, but over time KernelCash came up while in conversations with friends, family, and colleagues. Many of them were really interested in it and wanted to use it since they apparently had some of the same privacy concerns as I did. Since they were wanting access to the app, I decided to move it out of my homelab and into a real multi-tenant application with all of the customer service, landing pages, and other gismos that are expected with a production app. As expected, that was more work than the core app logic.We are priced lower than essentially all of the alternatives at $9.99/month or $87.50 for the annual subscription.If I had the financial means to, I would give this away for free. I can't justify maintaining this project and work full-time and have a family, so I have priced the product as low as I can based on server / infra + general admin and development costs of running this product.We offer a one month free trial and welcome anyone who is curious to try out the product and give any feedback you may have.Feel free to ask any questions, I would love to answer them!You can find KernelCash at https://kernelcash.comEdit: Fixed URL.

title: Show HN: Artificer by Nua: Frontier robotics task evaluation in 4B parameters
author: SunnyWan
body:
We’re happy to introduce Artificer, our first robotics decision model for evaluating robot task progress and success.
The problem
Robot systems need feedback during training, evaluation, and deployment. An arm might grasp the right object, but place it in the wrong bin. A robot might’ve only completed part of its task before it stopped. Assessing these outcomes from video often requires manual review or brittle, handcrafted objectives. Though frontier models do well in evaluation, they are expensive and slow. 
Artificer is a 4B parameter model that estimates task completion and progress, at the frontier level, from a task description and video. During deployment, these estimates provide feedback to a robot controller to help decide whether to continue an attempt, retry, or move to the next task.Know a robotics team working on task evaluation or success detection? We'd appreciate an introduction!
For the robotics founders: we’d love to test Artificer on your task videos! 
Would love to chat more in the comments or over email! sunny@trynua.dev

MAKE ROOM FOR THE WORK THAT MATTERS
 A clearer folder. A clearer next step.
 When everything lands in the same folder, finding the file you need becomes another task. Give the routine sorting a home, so you can get back to the work the files belong to.

01 Start with the work, not the cleanup.

What makes SortSage different

 01 Custom Rules Engine
 Match files by name, extension, type, size or age. Combine conditions and actions, or import custom rules as JSON.
02 Real-Time Folder Monitoring
 Watch local folders and sort new files using your rules. Keep SortSage in the system tray or run rules manually.

And there's more
 04

05 
 JSON Rules and AI Template
 Write custom JSON rules yourself or use the downloadable template with an AI of your choice. Review the imported rules before enabling them.
06 
 Local File Processing
 Organize files on your computer. Activate once through EnlightPixel, then keep working offline.
How SortSage works
 From setup to results, one step at a time.
 1 
 Define your rules
 Create rules, choose a copy-first starter or import custom JSON. You can optionally prepare JSON with an external AI using the included template.
2

Common questions about SortSage
 What can I organize with SortSage? Use rules to organize local files by name, extension, type, size or age. Combine conditions, preview actions and choose how collisions are handled. Content Contains searches plain text, not text inside PDFs, Word documents or images.
 Does SortSage move or copy files? Choose Move or Copy in your rules. The five starter rules keep originals by copying by default. Pause watching and use Dry Run before enabling new rules.
 Can SortSage undo every operation? No. Activity History supports undo for supported operations, most recent first, and persists across restarts. Permanent deletion and external script/application effects cannot be undone. Undo stops if the original location is occupied or destination size or modification time changed. Recycle and overwrite backups share 256 MiB; clearing history discards them. Keep a separate backup of important files.
 Does the AI template mean SortSage uses AI? No. SortSage runs local rules and has no built-in AI connection. You can edit JSON yourself or give the downloadable template to an external AI of your choice, then import and review its output. Anything you choose to share with that external service is separate from SortSage.
 What does Dry Run show? A snapshot of up to 1,000 predicted actions without changing files. Pause watching while reviewing because live monitoring can resume after preview generation. Scripts, collision-prompt answers and later file changes can affect actual results.
 Can I run SortSage on startup? Yes. Enable launch at Windows sign-in to start in the background. Closing the window keeps it in the system tray; choose Quit to exit.
 What happens if a file with the same name already exists? Choose SmartRename, Rename, Overwrite, Skip or Ask. SmartRename skips identical colliding contents and retains the source; otherwise it keeps both with a numbered name. Overwrite requires space to preserve the existing destination in undo storage.

title: Show HN: Post-Quantum Signatureless Authorization
author: ignotusnemo
body: Published: 2026-10-29 Author: Nemo, Ignotus Post-Quantum Signatureless Authorization | Zenodo Published October 29, 2026 | Version 1.0.0 Preprint Open ### Authors/Creators - Nemo, Ignotus ## Description Digital signatures authorize transactions, commands and other requests. Quantum attacks threaten widely used signature schemes, while their post-quantum replacements can be costly to verify inside proofs of execution. Signatureless authorization binds knowledge of an authority secret to a canonical request through a freshly randomized proof capsule. The public statement consists of a request identifier and a 32-byte authority commitment. Application rules enforce context, policy and freshness. The interface supports standalone requests and recursive proof composition. The construction combines a masked degree-ten authority reduction over GF(2^128), embedded in GF(2^256), with a bank-and-companion code proof. Source restoration gives expected polynomial-time public-coin extraction. An adaptive witness-free simulator and a same-experiment source extractor establish a quantum chosen-request authorization reduction in the stated address-compatible random-completion model. The public authority circuit and its address input slice are fixed. One permutation supplies the native transcript and commitments. Finite orbit-profile and resource conditions are explicit. The reduction quantifies simulation and extraction losses alongside authority-preimage hardness and canonical intent binding. For S <= T and T <= 2^24 charged native calls, the combined simulation and extraction loss is below 2^-67, including the uniform-slice setup failure. Parano1d supplies a blockchain implementation and recursive verifier. Canonical capsules are bounded by 92,696 bytes. On four CPU threads, median proving takes 0.81 to 0.89 seconds and verification takes approximately 25.6 milliseconds for two request fixtures. The accompanying reproducibility archive contains the manuscript sources, exact arithmetic and finite operator checks, simulation tests, recorded measurements, Rust reproduction programs and authenticated production source files. Its README provides the reproduction commands. Contact: dev@parano1d.org License information: The paper and accompanying written documentation are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Original software in the reproducibility artifact is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. Third-party dependencies retain their respective licenses. ## Files Post-Quantum Signatureless Authorization Ignotus Nemo dev@parano1d.org 29 October 2026 Abstract Digital signatures authorize transactions, commands and other requests. Quantum attacks threaten widely used signature schemes. Their post-quantum replacements can be costly to verify inside proofs of execution. Signatureless authorization binds knowledge of an authority secret to a canonical request through a freshly randomized proof capsule. The public statement consists of a request identiﬁer and a 32-byte authority commitment. Application rules enforce context, policy and freshness. The interface supports standalone requests and recursive proof composition. The construction combines a masked degree-ten authority reduction over F 2 128 ⊂ F 2 256 with a bank-and-companion code proof. Source restoration gives expected polynomial-time public-coin extraction with error at most 5− 65 + 701202001642/ 2 255. The native model ﬁxes the public authority circuit and its address input slice, then samples a uniform permutation completion elsewhere. Under explicit ﬁnite orbit-proﬁle con- ditions, classical authorization requests and coherent forward and inverse queries admit the bound Pr[Forge Q] ≤ Adv Q pre +ε Q sim + ε Q ext + ε Q id. An adaptive witness-free simulator and ex- pected polynomial-time source extractor give explicit error terms for the shared native tran- script and commitment permutation. The source bank proves the ﬁxed authority circuit’s relation. For the ideal 256-bit authority-preimage task, constant-success generic quantum search has query scale 2 128. Parano1d supplies a blockchain implementation and recursive veriﬁer. It uses a 2,048-cell bank and 65 code queries, with canonical capsules bounded by 92,696 bytes. On four CPU threads, median proving takes 0.81 to 0.89 seconds and veriﬁcation takes approximately 25.6 milliseconds for two request ﬁxtures. 1 Introduction Quantum algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms threaten authorization based on these problems [Sho95]. NIST identiﬁes aﬀected standards and post-quantum replacements [MPR+ 26]. The ML-DSA parameter sets in FIPS 204 use 1,312 to 2,592-byte public keys and 2,420 to 4,627-byte signatures [Nat24a]. SLH-DSA signatures in FIPS 205 occupy 7,856 to 49,856 bytes [Nat24b]. Applications that certify both authorization and execution must also represent authorization veriﬁcation in their proof arithmetic. Post-quantum Privacy Pass studies this coupling through STARK-oriented Dilithium [PWFHW23]. This motivates the following design question: how to bind each request to its authority within the same arithmetic used to prove execution, while protecting a reusable secret across repeated authorizations. The resulting relation must also support recursive veriﬁcation and a stable boundary between authority and public execution. We therefore consider a direct proof of knowledge of an authority secret. Signatureless authorization binds freshly randomized proofs of knowledge of an authority secret to canonical requests. For intent I, identiﬁer m = ID(I) and required 32-byte authority commitment a, the public statement and authority relation are x = (m, a), R own(a, s) = [Addr(s) = a]. title: Show HN: OpenArcanum – An End-to-End Encrypted Alternative to Discord
author: SamInTheShell
body:
A while back I recall being told it can't be done and won't be "Discord". To that, I have to admit, it's not Discord. It isn't designed in a way to profile it's users and it respects privacy.There is still much work to do on this project, but it's in open beta with a web client so people can see how it works before committing to a desktop app download.
Mobile apps will come later, if there is proven interest in this platform.I don't care to monitize it. The only thing users will ever see is a non-intrusive "Please donate" badge at most, with the intentions to just keep the maintainer nodes and some official relays running.There are no accounts. There is no way for me to see the messages. Which iPhones does it work with? 
Sidekeys is built for iPhone Duo's big inner screen, and it works on any iPhone or iPad. On iPhone Duo it also works on the outer screen.
Can I use my iPhone as a second monitor for my Mac? 
Yes. Apple's Sidecar only works with iPad, so Sidekeys fills the gap: install the free Mac app, plug in your iPhone, and your Mac gets a real extra display you can drag windows onto, with touch, scrolling and typing. It works on iPad too.
How is Sidekeys different from Sidecar and iPhone Mirroring? 
Sidecar turns an iPad into a Mac display, but not an iPhone. iPhone Mirroring goes the other way, showing your iPhone on your Mac. Sidekeys puts your Mac's screen on your iPhone or iPad, and adds a control deck for the app you're using and a dashboard for AI coding agents.
Does it work with Claude Code? 
Yes. In the Mac app's menu, choose Agents, then Connect Claude Code. Every Claude Code session appears as a card on your phone, and you can approve or deny permission requests with one tap, seeing the actual command. If your phone isn't connected, approvals fall back to the normal terminal prompt.
Cable or Wi-Fi? 
Either. A USB-C cable gives the lowest delay; use one that carries data, not a charge-only one. Over Wi-Fi, pair once (plug in the cable once, or type the code your iPhone shows), and from then on your iPhone connects on its own whenever Sidekeys is open nearby. Wi-Fi connections are encrypted end to end between your two devices.
Which Macs are supported? 
A Mac with Apple silicon running macOS 27 or later, with the free Sidekeys app for Mac installed. Download it here .
The Mac app isn't on the Mac App Store because it creates a virtual display, which the Mac App Store doesn't allow. It's notarized by Apple and downloads straight from this site.
Is it a subscription? 
No. Try every feature free for 7 days, then unlock Sidekeys once for $9.99. No subscription, no account.
Can my family use it? 
Yes. The unlock works with Family Sharing, so people in your Apple Family Sharing group can use it too.
What happens to my data? 
Your screen, touches and typing never leave your own devices: they go directly between your iPhone and your Mac. The apps have no analytics, ads, tracking or accounts. If you buy on the web or join the beta list, we keep only your email and purchase. Read the privacy policy .

title: Show HN: Sunlight – the camera-based infinite canvas window manager for Mac
author: darindd
body: Hey HN, I'm Darin. You might know me from my work at Webflow (YC S13) and currently Ploy (YC P26).Sunlight is the way I imagined the Mac working before I got my 1st-gen MacBook Air in high school (2008). I had looked at a bunch of Apple videos of Mission Control (Exposé back then) and somehow decided it worked like an infinite canvas. I even told my mom about it! I guess it stuck with me.Windowing on the Mac is so good it's one of those "if it ain't broke don't fix it" things. And yet, it always felt lacking. title: Show HN: GenesisDB – The event sourcing database, is now open source
author: patriceckhart
body:
Docs Get started Blog 
 Support GitHub 
All posts PE Patric Eckhart 
 / October 24, 2026 
 GenesisDB 2.0 is Open Source
 MIT licensed, drop-in compatible and free for everyone .
 Today GenesisDB 2.0 is released, and with it the complete source code. The server, every SDK and the VS Code extension are now on GitHub under the MIT license.
 What changes for you
 No more Community and Enterprise editions. There is one GenesisDB, and it has every feature.
 No license keys, no event limits, no subscriptions.
 Use it commercially, modify it, embed it, redistribute it.
Why open source
 A database is a long-term decision. You put your history into it, and with event sourcing that history is the system. Nobody should have to wonder whether the vendor behind their event store will still be there in ten years. With the code in the open, that question goes away: GenesisDB belongs to everyone who builds with it.
 What is in 2.0
 One static binary: written in Go, standard library only in the engines, no runtime dependencies.
 CloudEvents native: every event is a CloudEvents 1.0 record in a hierarchical subject tree.
 Preconditions: atomic batch commits guarded by isSubjectNew , isSubjectExisting and isQueryResultTrue .
 GDBQL: filters, ordering, grouping, aggregates, projections and subqueries.
 Live subscriptions: history plus new events over Server-Sent Events.
 Hash chain: every event is SHA-256 chained to its predecessor and the whole store can be audited with one request.
 GDPR erasure: personal data in reference payloads is erased with one request, the hash chain stays valid and an audit trail is written.
 Operations: logical backup and restore, index rebuild, Prometheus and OpenTelemetry metrics, separate read and write tokens, TLS.
 Embeddable: store.Open(dir) runs the database inside your own Go program.
 Upgrading from 1.x
 GenesisDB 2.0 is a drop-in replacement for 1.x. Start it on an existing data directory and it migrates it on the first start. Every 1.x backup restores. Every 1.x route still answers with the same status and body, so existing clients keep working while you move to the new SDKs at your own pace. Your existing 1.x installations also keep running as before.
 A backup is mandatory. As with every migration, a backup before upgrading is not a recommendation but a requirement. The migration is one-way, so stop 1.x and copy the complete data directory before GenesisDB 2 starts on it for the first time. Without that copy there is no way back to 1.x.
 The only required configuration change: GENESISDB_AUTH_TOKEN now needs at least 32 bytes. The upgrade guide has all the details.
 Try it
bash 
 docker run --rm --name genesisdb \ 
 -e GENESISDB_AUTH_TOKEN="$( openssl rand -hex 32 )" \ 
 -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \ 
 -v genesisdb-data:/app/data \ 
 genesisdb/genesisdb:latest 
Then follow the quickstart . If something breaks, open an issue. If you want to make GenesisDB better, send a pull request.
 Thank you to everyone who used GenesisDB 1.x, reported problems and shaped what 2.0 became. This one is yours.

 MIT licensed event sourcing database. One binary, every feature.

title: Show HN: DissPair APK– Portable BLE and Bluetooth Classic Security Testing
author: threadpoolx
body:
GitHub - threadpoolx/DissPair: A native Android application built with Kotlin & Jetpack Compose for security testing Bluetooth Classic and BLE in authorized lab environments. · GitHub

## About

A native Android application built with Kotlin & Jetpack Compose for security testing Bluetooth Classic and BLE in authorized lab environments.

## Folders and files

| gradle.properties | gradle.properties | Downgrade to Gradle 8.14 / AGP 8.7.3 for F-Droid reproducible builds | Jun 11, 2026 |
| gradlew | gradlew | Complete rewrite to Native Kotlin Android and added GitHub Safety Com… | Apr 12, 2026 |
| gradlew.bat | gradlew.bat | Complete rewrite to Native Kotlin Android and added GitHub Safety Com… | Apr 12, 2026 |

| View all files | | | |

### Bluetooth Security Toolkit

A multi-platform educational toolkit for understanding Bluetooth Classic (RFCOMM) and BLE (GATT) protocol behavior in controlled, authorized lab environments.

 

> ⚠️
> 
> Authorized Use Only This toolkit is intended strictly for use on devices you personally own or have explicit written permission to test. Unauthorized use against third-party devices may violate local and international law. The authors assume no liability for misuse.
> 
> ⚠️
> 
> Potentially Harmful Capabilities & Risk Disclosure
> 
> This tool contains features that can cause operational disruption to target hardware if used improperly:
> 
> 1. RFCOMM Hardware Flooding: The "Flood" module intentionally injects dense byte streams into targeted Bluetooth channels. On vulnerable, legacy, or unpatched Bluetooth stacks, this can cause buffer overflows, resulting in the target device freezing, kernel panics, or complete Denial of Service (DoS).
> 2. Payload Injection & State Manipulation: The ability to inject raw AT commands (e.g., HFP handshake manipulation) and OBEX payloads can alter the operational state of target devices, potentially causing unauthorized call manipulation or disrupting audio gateways.
> 3. GATT Interaction: Unauthenticated reading/writing of BLE characteristics may expose sensitive plaintext data or alter IoT device configurations.
> 
> Use exclusively on hardware you own or have explicit consent to audit.

## What is DissPair?

DissPair is a Bluetooth security learning toolkit designed for students, hardware developers, and security researchers to explore low-level behavior of:

- Bluetooth Classic (RFCOMM)
- Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE GATT)

Unlike many tools that rely purely on Service Discovery Protocol (SDP), DissPair actively probes and interacts with devices to reveal real behavior vs advertised behavior.

It is designed for use in personal lab environments — testing your own devices, understanding protocol fundamentals, and learning how Bluetooth service discovery and channel communication works under the hood.

### CVEs Discovered using DissPair

| CVE Number | Vulnerability Description | Link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2026-31280 | An issue in the Bluetooth RFCOMM service of Parani M10 Motorcycle Intercom v2.1.3 allows unauthorized attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via supplying crafted RFCOMM frames. | View Details |
| CVE-2025-67133 | An issue in Hero Motocorp Vida V1 Pro 2.0.7 allows a local attacker to cause a denial of service via the BLE component | View Details |

## Platform Variants

| | Platform | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 📱 | Android | Native Kotlin app with Jetpack Compose UI for on-device Bluetooth analysis. Field learning — explore Bluetooth environments from a mobile device. |
| 🐧 | Linux CLI | Python-based tool using BlueZ and raw Bluetooth sockets. Desktop study — terminal-based protocol analysis with minimal dependencies. |

## Core Workflow

```
Scan   →  Discover nearby Bluetooth devices (Classic BR/EDR and BLE)
  ↓
Sweep  →  Probe RFCOMM channels (1–30) on your own device
  ↓
Map    →  Identify active vs advertised services
  ↓
Analyze → Interact with protocols (RFCOMM / GATT) to study behavior

```

## Who Is This For?

- Students learning Bluetooth protocol internals on their own hardware
- Hardware hobbyists auditing and validating their own devices
- Security researchers studying RFCOMM/GATT behavior in lab setups
- Developers building Bluetooth-enabled hardware who want to validate their own implementations

## Overview

DissPair APK is a native Android application written in Kotlin with a Jetpack Compose UI. It uses Android's native Bluetooth APIs directly — including `BluetoothAdapter`, `BluetoothGatt`, and reflection-based `createRfcommSocket` / `createInsecureRfcommSocket` calls — to interact with the device's Bluetooth stack without relying on higher-level abstractions.

## Repository Structure

```
Disspair/
├── app/
│   └── src/
│       └── main/
│           ├── java/org/disspair/disspair/
│           │   └── MainActivity.kt        # Core app logic, UI, Bluetooth analysis
│           └── res/
│               └── drawable/
│                   └── disspair_logo.png  # App icon
├── build.gradle
└── README.md

```

## Requirements

- Android 6.0 (API 23) or higher
- Android 12+ (API 31) requires `BLUETOOTH_SCAN` and `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT` permissions
- Location services must be enabled for Bluetooth scanning
- For Classic device analysis: Location + Nearby Devices permissions

### Direct Install (Pre-Built APK)

1. Download `disspair.apk` from the Releases tab
2. On your Android device, allow your browser or file manager to Install unknown apps
3. Open the app and grant the requested Location and Nearby Devices permissions

> These permissions are required for Bluetooth scanning on Android 12+

#### 1. Clone the Repository

```
git clone https://github.com/threadpoolx/DissPair.git
cd DissPair
git checkout APK
```

#### 2. Open in Android Studio

- Open Android Studio (Hedgehog or newer recommended)
- Select Open and navigate to the cloned directory
- Let Gradle sync complete

#### 3. Build & Run

```
# Via Android Studio: Build > Build Bundle(s) / APK(s) > Build APK(s)

# Or via command line:
./gradlew assembleDebug
```

The compiled APK will appear in `app/build/outputs/apk/debug/`.

> Ensure you have Android SDK, Android NDK, and JDK 17 installed and configured in Android Studio.

## How It Works

```
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as DissPair v2 (Android)
    participant B as Android BT Stack
    participant T as Target Device

    Note over D, T: 1. Setup & Device Discovery
    D->>B: checkPermissions() and startDiscovery()
    B-->>D: onDeviceFound(Name, MAC, Type)
    D->>D: UI Update - Categorize Classic vs BLE

    Note over D, T: 2. Classic RFCOMM & Payload Mapping
    D->>T: createRfcommSocket(ch 1-30)
    T-->>D: Socket Verified Open

    Note over D, T: Classic Attack Engine
    alt Method - Flood
        D->>T: write payload in High-Speed Loop
        T-->>D: IOException (Buffer Overflow / DoS)
    else Method - Payload Injection
        Note right of D: Feature - TTY (AT Cmds), PBAP, or Custom
        D->>T: Send specific Protocol Payload
        T-->>D: Stream Response / Data Leak
    end

    Note over D, T: 3. BLE GATT & Profile Interaction
    D->>T: connectGatt() and discoverServices()
    T-->>D: onServicesDiscovered(List of GattService)

    Note over D, T: BLE Attack Engine
    alt General Profile Access
        D->>T: readCharacteristic(Generic_UUID)
        T-->>D: onCharacteristicRead (DeviceInfo/Battery)
    else Customized Profile Manipulation
        Note right of D: Targeted Write/Fuzzing
        D->>T: writeCharacteristic(Custom_UUID, malformed_data)
        T-->>D: onCharacteristicWrite status
    end

    Note over D: closeAll() - Release Hardware Resources

```

### Device Discovery

| Button | Description |
| --- | --- |
| SCAN CLASSIC | Discovers nearby BR/EDR devices using Android's `startDiscovery` API. Loops up to 5 scan cycles to maximize coverage. |
| SCAN BLE | Passively listens for BLE advertisement packets via `BluetoothLeScanner`. |

Paired devices are loaded automatically from the local Bluetooth bond cache on startup and shown via the Paired toggle.

### Classic Analysis (RFCOMM)

Tap ANALYSE on any Classic or Paired device to open the RFCOMM Channel Analysis.

#### Channel Enumeration

Probes channels 1–15 by default (expandable to 16–30 via the `PROBE 16-30` button) using direct RFCOMM connection attempts. Reports which channels are live and whether they accept unpaired (insecure) or paired (secure) connections.

#### Per-Channel Actions

| Action | Description |
| --- | --- |
| PAYLOADS | Opens the payload dialog to send a predefined or custom payload to the channel |
| FLOOD | Transmits a continuous 2048-byte burst stream to stress-test the target's RFCOMM buffer handling |

#### Payload Dialog

- AT Command: Connect — Sends `ATZ\r\n` (Hayes modem reset/ping)
- PBAP/MAP: OBEX Connect — Sends a raw OBEX `0x80` Connect PDU
- Custom Payload — Enter any AT command; `\r\n` is auto-appended
- Includes automatic HFP handshake detection and bypass — if the target opens with an `AT+BRSF` prompt, the tool auto-negotiates with `AT+BRSF=0` before injecting the chosen payload

### GATT Analysis (BLE)

Tap ANALYSE on any BLE device to open the GATT Analysis.

- Establishes a GATT connection (LE transport) and enumerates all services and characteristics
- Displays service type (General for standard 16-bit Bluetooth UUIDs, Customized for vendor UUIDs) and full property flags (`R W WnR N I SW B EXT`)
- All GATT operations go through a serialised queue with timeouts, so rapid actions are never silently dropped by the Android stack
- ATT error codes are decoded by name (e.g. `INSUFFICIENT_AUTHENTICATION`, `INSUFFICIENT_ENCRYPTION`) instead of raw numbers
- Per-characteristic actions:

| Action | Description |
| --- | --- |
| READ | Reads the current value of the characteristic |
| WRITE | ASCII or raw Hex payload; write-with-response or write-without-response (also shown for write-without-response-only characteristics) |
| SUB / UNSUB | Enables notifications or indications via the CCCD and logs every incoming value with its UUID |

- The connection automatically requests the largest ATT MTU (517); the negotiated value is shown in the header, and payload limits follow it.
- Toolbar actions:

| Action | Description |
| --- | --- |
| AUDIT | Unauthenticated access audit (see below) |
| COPY / SHARE | Exports the last audit report as text |

#### GATT Access Audit

Tests what every characteristic allows without pairing and marks each one `OPEN`, `AUTH`, `ENC`, `AUTHZ`, `KEY`, `DENY` or `ERR` for read, subscribe and (optionally) write. Characteristics usable unpaired are flagged in red and summarised in an exportable report.

- Read and subscribe tests are non-destructive; subscriptions are disabled again after the test.
- Write test is one setting: Off (default), Echo only (rewrites the value just read on readable characteristics; write-only ones are skipped), or Echo + commit payload (write-only ones really get the hex payload you choose).
- Run it on an unbonded device. If Android shows a pairing prompt mid-audit, decline it; the report flags any bond-state change.
- Toggle HEX / ASCII display for all captured values

### Advertisement Inspector (GAP)

Tap ADV on any BLE device to inspect what it broadcasts, without connecting. It updates live while SCAN BLE runs.

- Every AD structure decoded: flags, UUID lists (with names), local name, TX power, appearance, service data, manufacturer data, Mesh, URI, connection interval range, and more. Malformed length fields are flagged.
- Vendor formats: Apple Continuity messages (iBeacon, AirDrop, Proximity Pairing, Handoff, Nearby Info/Action, Find My, ...), Eddystone UID/URL/TLM/EID, Google Fast Pair, Microsoft beacons, company-ID lookup.
- Privacy: address type (public / random static / resolvable private / non-resolvable; exact on Android 14+, best-guess earlier), stale private addresses, identifiers embedded in names, tracker beacons (Find My, SmartTag, Tile).
- Over time: estimated advertising interval, RSSI graph, number of distinct payloads (live state changes), legacy vs extended PDU, connectable flag, primary/secondary PHY, advertising SID.
- Risk flags: exposed DFU or Nordic UART services.
- COPY / SHARE a full text report; ANALYSE GATT jumps to the GATT screen.

BLE scanning now uses low-latency mode (and extended advertising where supported), so it uses more battery while a scan is running.

### Appearance

- Theme: follows the system light/dark setting by default. Tap the theme icon in the top bar to cycle System → Light → Dark; the choice is remembered. In light mode the neon log colours switch to darker shades that stay readable on white.
- Icon: launcher, adaptive (circle/squircle-safe) and in-app icons are generated from `disspair_logo_2.png`.

### System Log

A live scrolling terminal log at the top of the main screen and within each overlay shows all events, discovered targets, errors, and decoded responses in color-coded monospace output.

## Overview

A Python-based command-line tool using:

- Native Linux Bluetooth sockets (`AF_BLUETOOTH`)
- BlueZ stack

Allows low-level protocol interaction without abstractions.

## Supported Platforms

- Kali Linux (recommended)
- Ubuntu / Debian

> VM users must use a USB Bluetooth adapter

## Features & Workflow

```
flowchart TB
    Start["START: Init & Dep Check"] --> ScanClassic["Scan Classic\nhcitool/bluez"] & ScanBLE["Scan BLE\nBleak Scanner"] & PairedDevices["Paired Devices\nLocal BlueZ"] & ManualMAC["Manual MAC"]
    ScanClassic --> TargetLocked["Target Locked"]
    ScanBLE --> TargetLocked
    PairedDevices --> TargetLocked
    ManualMAC --> TargetLocked
    TargetLocked --> ClassicEnum["Classic Enumeration\nBrute-force RFCOMM 1-30"] & BLEEnum["BLE GATT Enumeration\nPull Services & Chars"]
    ClassicEnum --> ClassicAttacks["RFCOMM Attacks\n- Silent Connection\n- Kali TTY Modem Noise\n- Resource Flood DoS\n- Customized Payload"]
    BLEEnum --> BLEAttacks["GATT Interaction\n- Read Hex/ASCII\n- Write Text String\n- Write Raw Hex"]

```

### System Dependencies

```
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y bluez rfkill
```

### Python Setup

```
python3 -m venv disspair_env
source disspair_env/bin/activate
pip install bleak
```

## Usage

```
source disspair_env/bin/activate
sudo $(which python3) disspair_kali.py
```

### Step 1 — Discovery

- Scan Classic devices
- Scan BLE devices
- Load paired devices
- Manual MAC input

### Step 2 — Enumeration

- RFCOMM channel probing (1–30)
- BLE GATT enumeration

#### RFCOMM

- Connect to channel
- Send AT commands
- Flood testing

#### BLE

- Read characteristics
- Write characteristics

## Troubleshooting

```
sudo rfkill unblock bluetooth
sudo systemctl restart bluetooth
sudo hciconfig hci0 up
hciconfig -a
```

## Security & Abuse Reporting

If you need to report a security vulnerability, malicious activity, or third-party abuse related to this tool, please see the Security Policy for contact details and responsible disclosure guidelines.

## Legal & Ethical Use

Only use DissPair against:

- Devices you personally own
- Devices where you have explicit written authorization from the owner

Never use this tool against:

- Public devices
- Vehicles or infrastructure
- Third-party hardware without consent

title: Show HN: Pho – TUI for GitHub PRs
author: stag
body:
# utkarsh261/pho

TUI for Github Pull Requests

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 9
- Open issues: 0
- License: GNU General Public License v3.0
- Homepage: https://github.com/utkarsh261/pho
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-04-11T21:13:02Z

## Languages

- Go
- Just

## Topics

- github
- tui

## Top Contributors

- utkarsh261 (72 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 
 A TUI for GitHub pull requests.
 

 

## Features

- **Dashboard** - Auto-discovers repos, lists PRs across *My PRs*, *Needs Review*, *Involving*, and *Recent* tabs with a live preview pane.
- **Jump to repo/PR** - `Ctrl+P` to fuzzy-find and jump to any PR.
- **PR detail** - Browse description, diff, comments, and commits. Sidebar for files and CI checks.
- **Diff navigation** - Line-by-line cursor, `gg`/`G`, `Ctrl+d`/`Ctrl+u`, visual mode for selecting ranges.
- **Inline reviews** - Draft inline comments on diff lines, edit, discard, and batch-submit with a review event. Just like Github web UI.
- **Comments & approvals** - Post top-level comments, review comments, or approve directly.
- **PR actions** - Edit title/body, merge (with method selection), close/reopen, and checkout the branch locally.
- **Commit view** - Inspect individual commits and their diffs.
- **Search** - `/` to search within diffs and descriptions; `n`/`N` to jump between matches.

## Install

```
go install github.com/utkarsh261/pho/cmd/pho@latest
```

Binary lands in `$(go env GOPATH)/bin/pho`.

Or pin a specific version:

```
go install github.com/utkarsh261/pho/cmd/pho@v0.1.0
```

Add it to the `$PATH`:
```
echo 'export PATH="$(go env GOPATH)/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
````

## Usage

Right now, pho looks at only the `cwd` and its direct children directories (if they are actually git repos). So if you have some repositories cloned in a directory, you can either open pho in that directory or: 

```
$(go env GOPATH)/bin/pho ~/path/to/dir/containing/all/cloned/repositories
```
or simply start it in the current directory

```
pho
```

## Requirements

- Go 1.25+
- Git
- GitHub CLI (`gh`) — run `gh auth login` to authenticate

## Build

```
go build -o pho ./cmd/pho
```

With `just`:

```
just build
```

## Run

```
./pho
```

Flags:

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--version` | Print version and exit |
| `--debug` | Enable debug logging |
| `--reset` | Clear all caches and exit |
| `--config ` | Path to config file |
| `--root ` | Root directory to scan for git repos (default `.`) |

## Test

```
go test ./...
```

With `just`:

```
just test
```

## Vet

```
go vet ./...
```

With `just`:

```
just vet
```

## Logs

```
tail -f ~/.local/state/pho/debug.log
```

## Why
So that i can build it exactly how i want a tool which i use on a regular basis to be.

# The universal AI agent engine for PHP.

Tools, memory, security, and a ReAct loop, already built. Zero framework dependencies in core. Any LLM provider.

## First agent in seconds

```
composer require phpclaw/phpclaw
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
```

```
$agent = PhpClaw\Claw::builder()->build();
echo $agent->send('What can you help me with?')->text;
```

One env var, one builder, one `send()`. The builder checks `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, then `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GROQ_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `MISTRAL_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `OLLAMA_HOST`, in that order, and uses whichever it finds first. No YAML, no agent framework to learn, no vendor lock-in.

## Give your agent tools

An agent without tools can only talk. Register the ones your application needs and it starts doing real work:

```
use PhpClaw\Claw;
use PhpClaw\Tools\ShellTool;
use PhpClaw\Tools\HttpTool;
use PhpClaw\Tools\FileReadTool;
use PhpClaw\Tools\DatabaseQueryTool;
use PhpClaw\Tools\CodeSearchTool;

$agent = Claw::builder()
    ->tools([
        new ShellTool(allowlist: ['ls', 'df', 'tail']),
        new HttpTool(),
        new FileReadTool(),
        new DatabaseQueryTool($pdo),
        new CodeSearchTool(),
    ])
    ->build();
```

```
> Check disk usage and tail the last 20 lines of the error log
> Is api.example.com responding right now?
> Run a read-only SELECT to count today's orders
> Find every place UserService is used in this codebase

```

The agent decides which tools to call and in what order, running a ReAct loop (reason, act, observe, repeat) until it has an answer or hits the iteration cap. This works identically whether the tools touch your shell, your database, your HTTP APIs, or your codebase.

## Why phpClaw

Every "AI in PHP" tutorial ends the same way: an HTTP client bolted onto a provider API, a hand-rolled tool-call loop, and a prayer that the prompt holds up in production. A generic LLM SDK gives you the API client. phpClaw gives you the agent runtime around it: the loop, the guards, the memory, the framework wiring, already assembled.

| | phpClaw | Generic LLM SDK |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool-calling loop | ReAct, built in | You write it |
| Framework-native adapters | 8, idiomatic per framework | None |
| Prompt injection defence | 8 default guards + opt-in rate limiting | None |
| Memory abstraction | Swappable drivers | None |
| Streaming + tool-calls together | Hybrid mode | Varies |
| MCP server bundled | Expose any app to Claude Desktop | None |
| Chains and multi-agent graphs | `Pipeline` and `Graph`: loops, human pause and resume, fan-out | You build it |
| Zero framework deps in core | `ext-curl`, `ext-json`, `ext-mbstring`, done | Depends |
| Core license | MIT, nothing gated | Varies |

Not trying to be everything. phpClaw isn't a RAG framework: there are no embeddings or vector stores. It's built to give an LLM tools, memory and security controls against your real application, and to chain those agents into pipelines and graphs when one call isn't enough.

## What phpClaw provides

Agent runtime. A ReAct loop with a hard iteration cap (`max_iterations`, default 20), pluggable tools, pluggable memory, and skills the model loads on demand through the `load_skill` tool, all running inside a single reasoning cycle.

Pipelines and graphs. `Pipeline` chains steps (prompt template, agent, structured output, your own callables) with retry and fallback. `Graph` runs nodes that loop, branch, pause for a human, resume in another process, and fan out to branches that run inline or are drained by workers from cron, a queue or the CLI. See Pipelines and Graphs.

Provider flexibility. 7 providers auto-detected from environment variables: Anthropic, OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, Ollama. A custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint is also supported, opt-in via `PHPCLAW_PROVIDER=custom`. Switch providers with `->provider()` and `->model()`, no code changes elsewhere.

Production controls. 8 security guards on by default (prompt injection, PII, code injection, Unicode, homoglyph, role-switch, destructive SQL, message length), plus rate limiting available as an opt-in guard. Tool results are sanitised unconditionally by `ToolOutputGuard`, which sits outside the guard registry, and LLM output sanitisation is on by default and can be disabled with `->sanitiseOutput(false)`. `ShellTool` is allowlist-only with a hard-coded command blocklist that can't be overridden. `HttpTool` validates resolved IPs, not just hostnames, closing the DNS-rebinding gap a prefix blocklist alone would miss. `FileReadTool`/`FileWriteTool` are workspace-sandboxed and refuse sensitive paths and extensions.

Developer experience. Token-by-token streaming, prompt caching (cached input tokens billed at Anthropic's discounted cache-read rate, see Anthropic's pricing for the exact figure), and extended thinking (Claude's reasoning chain exposed on `$response->thinking`).

Ecosystem. 8 framework and CMS adapters, an MCP server for exposing your tools to Claude Desktop and Claude Code, and an optional cloud transport for a hosted, continuously-updated prompt-scan guard.

## Framework & CMS adapters

Each adapter wires phpClaw into its host's own idioms: Eloquent for Laravel, Doctrine for Symfony, WP-CLI for WordPress, Drush for Drupal, and so on. Every adapter ships an admin chat or CLI and the same 3-table memory schema underneath.

| Platform | Package | Install | Versions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Laravel | `phpclaw/phpclaw-laravel` | Composer | 10, 11, 12, 13 |
| Symfony | `phpclaw/phpclaw-symfony` | Composer | 6.4, 7.x, 8.x |
| Drupal | `phpclaw/phpclaw-drupal` | Composer | 10, 11 |
| Magento / Adobe Commerce | `phpclaw/phpclaw-magento` | Composer | 2.4.x |
| WordPress + WooCommerce | -- | ZIP upload | 6.2+ |
| Joomla | -- | ZIP upload | 4, 5, 6 |
| OpenCart | -- | ZIP upload | 3.x, 4.x |
| PrestaShop | -- | ZIP upload | 8.x, 9.x |

CMS adapters ship as ZIP downloads from Releases, not Composer, because that's how their host platforms install extensions.

```
php artisan phpclaw "deploy staging and notify #ops"          # Laravel
bin/console phpclaw "check all database connections"          # Symfony
drush phpclaw:run "list recently-active users"                # Drupal
bin/magento phpclaw:run "check order-queue status"             # Magento
wp phpclaw send "summarise today's posts"                     # WordPress
php cli/joomla.php phpclaw "list recent articles"              # Joomla
php cli/phpclaw.php send "check low stock products"            # OpenCart
php modules/phpclaw/cli/phpclaw.php send "check stock levels"  # PrestaShop
```

Full per-adapter reference (tools, REST routes, CLI commands, settings, memory drivers) lives on the doc site. Each adapter's own README is a short pointer, not a manual. Building a new one? See the community adapter guides.

## MCP Server

`phpclaw/phpclaw-mcp` exposes your existing `ToolRegistry` over the Model Context Protocol, so Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client can call your tools directly, with the default guards scanning every tool call's arguments (the prompt-only code-injection, PII and length guards apply to chat messages, not tool arguments). No changes to the tools themselves.

```
composer require phpclaw/phpclaw-mcp
```

Full quick start, transport, and security details: phpclaw.ai/docs/mcp.

## Security

Every message runs through the default guard chain before it reaches the provider. `ShellTool` runs only commands on its allowlist (default `ls`, `pwd`, `df`, `wc`, `date`, `uptime`, `hostname`, `whoami`), matched exactly and case-sensitively; a fixed, non-overridable blocklist of dangerous commands is checked first regardless of what's allowlisted. `HttpTool` blocks requests by hostname prefix, then re-validates every resolved IP address, catching CGNAT and DNS-rebinding attempts that hostname checks alone would miss. `FileReadTool` and `FileWriteTool` are sandboxed to a configured workspace root and refuse credentials, keys and security directories (`.git`, `.ssh`, `wp-admin`, ...) unconditionally, and `vendor/` and `node_modules/` by default.

Full guard reference, the exact `ShellTool` blocklist, and the SSRF/sandbox implementation details: phpclaw.ai/docs/security. Found a vulnerability? See SECURITY.md, do not open a public issue.

## Architecture

```
Message
  → Guards       (blocks injection/PII before the LLM sees it)
  → Hooks         (lifecycle events fire, 44 across the loop)
  → Agent          (ReAct loop: provider + tools + memory + skills)
  → AgentResponse  (text, tokens, tool calls, timing)

```

Providers, tools, memory, guards, and skills are all pluggable through registries; every adapter wires them from its own config or environment. Full architecture diagram and design rules: phpclaw.ai/docs/architecture.

## Extensibility

Five static registries (`GuardRegistry`, `HookRegistry`, `MemoryRegistry`, `ProviderRegistry`, `SkillRegistry`) plus the per-agent `ToolRegistry` instance. Drop a class in `packages/core/src/ /` with the matching attribute (`#[Tool]`, `#[Provider]`, `#[Memory]`, `#[Skill]`, `#[Hook]`, `#[Guard]`), run `composer dump-autoload`, it's live. Or register from code: `GuardRegistry::register()`, `HookRegistry::on()`, `$toolRegistry->register([...])`.

Full extension recipes with working code for every subsystem: phpclaw.ai/docs.

## Testing

```
for pkg in core cloud mcp; do (cd packages/$pkg && composer test); done
```

Unit tests use mocks and stubs for HTTP clients, `\Redis`, and the filesystem: no external network calls and no API keys are needed to run the suite for core, cloud, or mcp. The full testing rules, including how to test a core change through an adapter, are in the contributing guide.

## Documentation

This README gets you installed. Everything else, architecture, the full provider/tool/guard/hook/memory/skill reference, per-adapter tool and REST tables, code examples, upgrading, troubleshooting, lives at:

## Requirements

- PHP: 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, 8.4
- Extensions:`ext-curl`, `ext-json`, `ext-mbstring` (core only; adapters may need more, documented per-package)

## License

MIT, built with love for the PHP community. Part of the phpClaw project.

## About

Open-source AI agent framework for PHP. Tools, memory, security guards and a ReAct loop built in. Works with Laravel, Symfony, WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Joomla, OpenCart, PrestaShop. Any LLM provider. MIT.
